paragraphs.heading: What a cubic is
paragraphs.text: A cubic equation in one unknown has the shape ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0, where a must not be zero. The letters a, b, c and d are its four coefficients, and they do not have to be real numbers. The solutions, or roots, need not be the same kind of number as the coefficients. Some cubics with rational coefficients have roots that are irrational, or not even real.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to find the roots
paragraphs.text: Every cubic can be solved exactly by a cubic formula. That formula uses only the four coefficients, the four basic operations of arithmetic, square roots and cube roots. The same holds for equations of degree two and four, but not for higher degrees. When a close answer is enough, a root-finding method such as Newton's method can home in on the roots numerically.

paragraphs.heading: A very old problem
paragraphs.text: Babylonians, Greeks, Chinese, Indians and Egyptians all knew of cubic equations. Babylonian cuneiform tablets carry tables of cubes and cube roots, though no evidence shows they were used to solve cubics. The oldest cubic people studied comes from the puzzle of doubling the cube. In the 5th century BC Hippocrates turned it into a search for two mean proportionals between a line and one twice as long. He could not construct them with compass and straightedge, a task now known to be impossible.

paragraphs.heading: Methods across Asia and Europe
paragraphs.text: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, a Chinese text gathered around the 2nd century BC, contains methods for cubics. In the 7th century Wang Xiaotong set up and solved 25 cubics numerically. In the 12th century Sharaf al-Dīn al-Tūsī sorted cubics into types and approximated a root by what is now called the Horner–Ruffini method. He also used the highest and lowest points of curves to deal with cubics that might have no positive solution. Fibonacci closely approximated the positive root of x³ + 2x² + 10x = 20, with a relative error of about 10⁻⁹.

paragraphs.heading: Secrets and a contest
paragraphs.text: In the early 1500s Scipione del Ferro found how to solve cubics of the form x³ + mx = n. He kept it secret until just before he died, then told his student Antonio Fior. In 1535 Niccolò Tartaglia said he could solve two cubic problems sent to him, and Fior soon challenged him. Each put up money and set problems for the other, and whoever solved more in 30 days took it all. Tartaglia was given problems of the form x³ + mx = n, which he had a general method for. Fior got problems of the form x³ + mx² = n, could not solve them, and lost.

paragraphs.heading: A broken promise
paragraphs.text: Gerolamo Cardano talked Tartaglia into sharing his method in 1539, on the condition that Cardano would never reveal it. Years later Cardano learned of del Ferro's earlier work and printed that method in his book Ars Magna in 1545, crediting Tartaglia with solving it on his own. Tartaglia then challenged Cardano, who refused. Cardano's student Lodovico Ferrari took up the contest and did better, and Tartaglia lost both his standing and his income.

paragraphs.heading: Where complex numbers came from
paragraphs.text: Cardano saw that Tartaglia's method sometimes asked for the square root of a negative number. He even put such a calculation in Ars Magna without really understanding it. Rafael Bombelli worked through the problem in detail, and for that he is often called the discoverer of complex numbers. François Viète (1540–1603) found on his own a solution using trigonometry for cubics with three real roots, and René Descartes built on his work.
